specPoints.text: know that an addition polymer is formed by joining up many small molecules called monomers
understand how to draw the repeat unit of an addition polymer, including poly(ethene), poly(propene), poly(chloroethene) and (poly)tetrafluoroethene
understand how to deduce the structure of a monomer from the repeat unit of an addition polymer and vice versa

primer.text: You already know from Alkenes that the C=C double bond is reactive and can open up to add other atoms across it. Addition polymerisation is that same reactivity put to work on a grand scale, with each alkene opening to grip its neighbours. This note shows how the giant chains form, how to draw them, and how to read them backwards.

lessons.title: Monomers
lessons.opening: Polymers are the giant molecules behind plastics, polystyrene and nylon, and this lesson introduces their recipe. Every polymer is assembled from huge numbers of small starter molecules called monomers, linked end to end by covalent bonds. The reaction needs demanding conditions, and it comes in two natural varieties: manufactured and biological.
keyPoints: A polymer is a large molecule of high relative molecular mass, built from many joined monomers.
The process of joining monomers together is called addition polymerisation.
Each monomer becomes a repeat unit, connected to its neighbours by covalent bonds.
Polymerisation reactions usually need high pressures and a catalyst.
Synthetic polymers are manufactured, like plastics and nylon, while nature makes natural or biological polymers.

low.restatement: Many small monomer molecules join end to end into one long polymer chain of repeating units.
low.analogy: It is like clipping train carriages together: each carriage is a monomer, the couplings are covalent bonds, and the coupled line is the polymer.
low.examPointer: Expect to name everyday polymers, such as plastics and polystyrene, and to state what monomers are.

medium.restatement: Addition polymerisation links monomers through covalent bonds under high pressure with a catalyst, producing molecules of high relative molecular mass; the same chemistry occurs in nature as well as in factories.
medium.analogy: Think of a paper chain: each loop is a monomer, the staples are covalent bonds, and the finished garland is far longer than any single loop.
medium.examPointer: Keep the terms straight: the monomer is the starter molecule, and the repeat unit is its pattern inside the chain.

options.text: A small molecule that joins with many others to build a polymer
options.explanation: The word means one part; monomers are the building blocks of the chain.

options.text: A large molecule of high relative molecular mass
options.explanation: That describes the polymer, the product, not its starting blocks.

options.text: The bond that links two polymer chains
options.explanation: Monomers are molecules, not bonds.

options.text: The repeat unit as it appears in the finished chain
options.explanation: The monomer is the free starting molecule; the repeat unit is its pattern inside the chain.

check.stem: Which bonds connect each repeat unit to its neighbours?

options.text: Covalent bonds
options.explanation: The note states adjacent units connect via covalent bonds.

options.text: Ionic bonds
options.explanation: Ionic bonding needs ions; polymers are covalently linked molecules.

options.text: Hydrogen bonds
options.explanation: Attractions between molecules are not the links that build the chain.

options.text: Metallic bonds
options.explanation: Metallic bonding involves metal atoms, not organic monomers.

check.stem: Which statement about polymer sources matches the note?

options.text: Synthetic polymers are manufactured, and nature also produces its own polymers
options.explanation: Both sources exist: factories make plastics and nylon, while nature makes biological polymers.

options.text: All polymers are manufactured in industry
options.explanation: Nature also produces polymers, called natural or biological.

options.text: All polymers are found ready-made in nature
options.explanation: Many, such as plastics and nylon, are manufactured.

options.text: Natural and synthetic polymers have no shared name
options.explanation: Both are polymers; the labels only record where they come from.

check.stem: What conditions do polymerisation reactions usually require?

options.text: High pressures and a catalyst
options.explanation: Those are the note's two stated requirements.

options.text: Very low temperatures
options.explanation: Low temperature is not stated; pressure and catalyst are.

options.text: Strong acids as the catalyst
options.explanation: The note names a catalyst without specifying an acid.

options.text: Sunlight and exposure to air
options.explanation: Neither appears in the note's conditions.

check.stem: Plastics, polystyrene and nylon are all examples of what?

options.text: Everyday materials that are polymers
options.explanation: The note lists exactly these as everyday polymer materials.

options.text: Monomers awaiting polymerisation
options.explanation: They are finished polymer materials, not starters.

options.text: Natural polymers
options.explanation: They are manufactured, which makes them synthetic.

options.text: Catalysts for polymerisation
options.explanation: They are products, not reaction helpers.

lessons.title: Drawing polymers
lessons.opening: The second lesson turns to drawing: how a stream of alkene monomers becomes a polymer chain on paper. The trick is the C=C double bond, which opens up to link each monomer to its neighbours. Naming follows a simple pattern too, with poly- fixed to the front of the monomer's name.
keyPoints: Addition polymerisation only works with monomers that contain a C=C double bond.
One of the two bonds in each C=C breaks, forming the bond to the adjacent monomer.
The resulting polymer chain contains single bonds only.
The polymer's name takes the monomer's name in brackets with poly- added in front.
Propene monomers form polypropene, and ethene monomers form polyethene, as the note's two examples.

low.restatement: The C=C double bond in each monomer opens, one of its two bonds links to the next monomer, and the chain that results has only single bonds.
low.analogy: Picture velcro strips: only strips with the hook side can join, and once joined the hooks are used up, leaving smooth fabric along the chain.
low.examPointer: Practise all four named polymers: poly(ethene), poly(propene), poly(chloroethene) and (poly)tetrafluoroethene.

medium.restatement: Only monomers carrying a C=C bond can add to the chain, because breaking one bond of the pair frees each end to bond to neighbours; groups attached to the alkene simply ride along, and naming brackets the monomer name behind poly-.
medium.analogy: Think of unzipping a jacket halfway: the opened teeth fasten onto the next jacket, and the embroidered patches hang wherever they started.
medium.examPointer: In diagrams, make sure one of the two C=C bonds is the one shown breaking, and that the polymer shows single bonds throughout.

check.stem: Which structural feature must a monomer have for addition polymerisation?

options.text: A C=C double bond
options.explanation: Only monomers containing a C=C bond take part in addition polymerisation.

options.text: A C-C single bond
options.explanation: Single bonds cannot open to link; the double bond is the requirement.

options.text: A chlorine atom attached
options.explanation: Chlorine is one possible attached group, not the requirement.

options.text: An O-H group
options.explanation: A hydroxyl group is another possible rider, not the entry ticket.

check.stem: What happens to one of the two bonds in each C=C during polymerisation?

options.text: It breaks and forms the bond with the adjacent monomer
options.explanation: One bond of the pair opens outward to link the chain.

options.text: It strengthens and shortens
options.explanation: The bond is consumed in linking, not reinforced.

options.text: It turns the molecule into an ion
options.explanation: No ions form; the electrons go into a new covalent bond.

options.text: It disappears completely without doing anything
options.explanation: The broken bond becomes the link to the neighbour.

check.stem: What kinds of bonds does the finished polymer chain contain?

options.text: Single bonds only
options.explanation: The opened double bonds all become single bonds in the chain.

options.text: Double bonds throughout
options.explanation: Each monomer's double bond opened to join the chain.

options.text: Alternating single and double bonds
options.explanation: No double bonds remain in an addition polymer's backbone.

options.text: No bonds between the units
options.explanation: Covalent bonds join every adjacent unit.

check.stem: How is the polymer's name built from the monomer's name?

options.text: Put the monomer's name in brackets and add poly- in front
options.explanation: That is the note's stated naming rule.

options.text: Add -ide to the end of the monomer's name
options.explanation: That suffix belongs to ionic compounds, not polymers.

options.text: Use the monomer's name with no changes
options.explanation: The poly- prefix marks the substance as a polymer.

options.text: Reverse the letters of the monomer's name
options.explanation: No reversal occurs; only the prefix and brackets are added.

check.stem: Propene undergoes addition polymerisation. What is the product's name?

options.text: Polypropene
options.explanation: The note gives exactly this pairing as an example.

options.text: Propenide
options.explanation: The -ide suffix does not make polymer names.

options.text: Polyethene
options.explanation: Polyethene comes from ethene, a different monomer.

options.text: Propane
options.explanation: Propane is a small alkane, not a polymer of propene.

lessons.title: Deducing monomers and repeat units
lessons.opening: The final skill runs in both directions: given a monomer, draw the repeat unit; given a repeat unit, recover the monomer. Three changes do all the work — swap the bond order, adjust the end bonds, and mind the subscript n. Get those right and every named polymer is within reach.
keyPoints: To draw a repeat unit, change the monomer's double bond to a single bond.
Add a bond to each end, and let them extend outside the brackets.
A subscript n on the bottom right shows that a large number of repeat units are present.
The other groups keep the same order they had around the double bond in the monomer.
To recover the monomer, change the single bond back to a double bond and remove the end bonds and the n.

low.restatement: Monomer to repeat unit: the double bond becomes single, add extension bonds past the brackets and the subscript n; repeat unit to monomer: reverse the steps.
low.analogy: It works like a two-way recipe: fold a page in half, tuck the ends under the clip, and unfold the same page again to recover it.
low.examPointer: The commonest mark loss is forgetting the extension bonds outside the brackets or the subscript n, so check both every time.

medium.restatement: The monomer's double bond and the repeat unit's single bond are the same linkage in two states: converting one to the other, adding or removing the end bonds and the subscript n, is the entire change, with every attached group kept in order.
medium.analogy: Picture a zip on a backpack: zipped is the repeat unit with its extension bonds, unzipped is the monomer with its double bond, and the same teeth change state without rearranging.
medium.examPointer: Deduce monomers from repeat units by reopening the double bond exactly between the two bracketed carbons, keeping attached groups in the same positions.

check.stem: When drawing a repeat unit from a monomer, what happens to the double bond?

options.text: It becomes a single bond in the repeat unit
options.explanation: The note's rule: double in the monomer, single in the repeat unit.

options.text: It stays a double bond
options.explanation: Keeping the double bond is the classic error; polymerisation consumed it.

options.text: It becomes a triple bond
options.explanation: Nothing in this transformation produces a triple bond.

options.text: It moves to the other end of the molecule
options.explanation: The bond changes order in place; it does not migrate.

check.stem: What must be drawn at each end of the repeat unit?

options.text: A bond extending outside each bracket
options.explanation: The extension or continuation bonds show the chain carrying on.

options.text: Nothing beyond the brackets
options.explanation: Bare brackets lose the mark; the bonds must extend outside.

options.text: A duplicate of the whole unit
options.explanation: The subscript n already says the unit repeats.

options.text: A capital N in the top corner
options.explanation: The marker is a small subscript n at the bottom right.

check.stem: What does the subscript n represent?

options.text: A large number of repeat units in the chain
options.explanation: The n stands for the many units linked together.

options.text: The number of double bonds left
options.explanation: No double bonds remain in the repeat unit.

options.text: The monomer's group number
options.explanation: Group numbers do not appear here.

options.text: The polymer's overall charge
options.explanation: The chain is neutral; n counts units, not charge.

check.stem: When recovering the monomer from a repeat unit, which changes do you make?

options.text: Change the single bond back to a double bond, remove the end bonds and the subscript n
options.explanation: That is the note's three-part reverse procedure.

options.text: Change the single bond to a triple bond
options.explanation: The monomer's bond is double, not triple.

options.text: Add a second subscript n in front of the monomer
options.explanation: The n is removed from the bracket and may be written before the monomer, not added twice.

options.text: Leave the end bonds attached to the monomer
options.explanation: The end bonds belong to the repeat unit only.

check.stem: You are given a repeat unit and asked for its monomer. What is the key step?

options.text: Reopen a double bond between the two carbons the brackets enclose, keeping the attached groups in place
options.explanation: The monomer is the repeat unit with the double bond restored.

options.text: Add two extra carbons to the chain
options.explanation: No carbons are added; the unit already holds the monomer's skeleton.

options.text: Break the chain into separate single atoms
options.explanation: The monomer stays a whole molecule.

options.text: Replace the attached groups with hydrogen
options.explanation: The attached groups, such as chlorine, stay exactly where they are.

glossary.definition: A small molecule that joins with many others to build a polymer.
A large molecule of high relative molecular mass made from linked monomers.
The process of joining many monomers into a polymer; with C=C monomers it is called addition polymerisation.
The pattern of one monomer as it appears inside the polymer chain.
Made by people; synthetic polymers such as plastics are manufactured rather than found in nature.
The bonds drawn sticking out beyond the brackets of a repeat unit, showing the chain continues.

workedExample.prompt: a) Propene monomers form polypropene. Describe the three changes needed to draw the repeat unit from the monomer. b) State what the C=C bond contributes to addition polymerisation. c) How would you recover the monomer from the repeat unit of poly(chloroethene)?
steps: a) Change the monomer's C=C double bond to a single bond; add an extension (continuation) bond to each end, extending outside the brackets; add the subscript n at the bottom right — the other groups keep the same order they had around the double bond.
b) Only monomers containing a C=C bond can undergo addition polymerisation: one of the two bonds in each C=C breaks to bond to the adjacent monomer, and the polymer chain contains single bonds only.
c) Change the repeat unit's single bond back to a double bond, remove the end extension bonds and the subscript n — the monomer chloroethene remains.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Double bond becomes single; extension bonds outside brackets; subscript n. b) The C=C is required and one of its bonds breaks; the chain is all single bonds. c) Reopen the double bond and remove the end bonds and n.
